section_1.title: Introduction: The 'Bell Curve' Phenomenon
section_1.content: Briefly define the Normal Distribution (Gaussian). Introduce the concept of independent variables as 'building blocks'. Visualize a single bell curve transforming into a sharper/wider bell curve when we shift parameters (mean and variance).
section_1.example: A delivery robot travels from point A to point B. Its total time is the sum of time taken for 'navigation' and 'obstacle avoidance', both of which follow normal distributions.

section_2.title: The Rule of Summation
section_2.content: State the core theorem: The sum of two independent normally distributed random variables X ~ N(μ₁, σ₁²) and Y ~ N(μ₂, σ₂²) results in a new random variable Z ~ N(μ₁+μ₂, σ₁²+σ₂²). Emphasize that the shape remains Gaussian.
section_2.example: Animation showing two separate bell curves sliding together. When combined, the mean shifts to the sum of the means, and the 'width' (variance) increases as the two distributions overlap.

section_3.title: Intuitive Visualization: The Combining Effects
section_3.content: Explain the mechanics: Adding means is straightforward (location shift). Adding variances is the critical part (spreading uncertainty). Use a graphic overlay showing the 'summed' curve being taller and wider than the individual components.
section_3.example: An archer shooting at a target. If the error of the arm movement (X) and the error of the wind (Y) are both Gaussian, the final impact point (Z) is still a Gaussian 'cloud' centered at the combined average.

section_4.title: Why It Matters: Applications
section_4.content: Discuss real-world utility: Noise reduction, signal processing, and error propagation. Emphasize that because the sum remains Gaussian, we can predict complex system behaviors using simple arithmetic.
section_4.example: A smart thermometer: It takes three separate sensor readings, each with Gaussian noise. Knowing the sum of Gaussians allows the device to calibrate its final output with high precision.

section_5.title: Summary and Pro-Tips
section_5.content: Recap: Means add up, variances add up. Cautionary note: This holds for independent variables; mention that dependence (covariance) changes the result, serving as a teaser for future lessons.
section_5.example: A quick visual animation: 'Input Gaussian 1 + Input Gaussian 2 = Resulting Gaussian'. A clean, 5-second final slide summarizing the two addition rules.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
